label: geo-square
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Ordered square

title: Proof
body_md:
Here $\widetilde\omega^2=4\omega_X\wedge\omega_{FS}$ and
$\Omega_{jj}=(I+iH_j)\omega_X+2(I+iS_j)\omega_{FS}$. Thus the diagonal
square, before including adjacent off-diagonal products, is
\[
 \tfrac12\big[(I+iH_j)(I+iS_j)+(I+iS_j)(I+iH_j)\big]
 =I+i(H_j+S_j)-\tfrac12\{H_j,S_j\}.
\]
For $\gamma_i=\xi_i\wedge\alpha$, graded multiplication gives
\[
 \gamma_i\wedge\gamma_i^\dagger
 =-2i\xi_i\wedge\xi_i^\dagger\wedge\omega_{FS},\qquad
 \gamma_i^\dagger\wedge\gamma_i
 =2i\xi_i^\dagger\wedge\xi_i\wedge\omega_{FS}.
\]
After division by $\widetilde\omega^2$ these contribute exactly
\eqref{geo-K}. A pure base or fiber $(1,1)$-form wedges to zero with each
mixed $\xi_i\wedge\alpha$, and the two consecutive mixed forms wedge to
zero because $\alpha\wedge\alpha=0$; the adjoint products behave likewise.
Products involving both $R_1$ and $P_2$ vanish by fiber form degree. These
facts remove every off-diagonal square block and retain the ordered middle
anticommutator. No commutation of the endomorphisms has been used.
head: environment

label: geo-domain
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{geo-domain}
There are precisely eleven nonempty triples
$(a,b,\epsilon)=(\operatorname{rank}A,\operatorname{rank}B,
\mathbf1_{\{Q\not\equiv0\}})$. They and exact representatives are listed
below, with $O=0$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$,
$D^\perp=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ and
$J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 (a,b,\epsilon)&A&B&Q(z)\\\hline
 (0,0,0)&O&O&0\\(0,1,0)&O&D&0\\(0,2,0)&O&I&0\\
 (1,0,0)&D&O&0\\(1,1,0)&D&D^\perp&0\\
 (1,1,1)&D&D&z_0^2\\(1,2,1)&D&I&z_0^2\\
 (2,0,0)&I&O&0\\(2,1,1)&I&D&z_0^2\\
 (2,2,0)&I&J&0\\(2,2,1)&I&I&z_0^2+z_1^2
\end{array}
\]
If $a=2,b=1$, the original lower map has the form
$\psi=v\sigma$, with saturated line $L=\mathcal O(2)v$,
$\operatorname{im}\psi=L(-p)$, and
$\operatorname{div}(\phi|_L)=q_0$ for simple divisor points $p,q_0$.
Then $\operatorname{div}Q=p+q_0$, allowing $p=q_0$.
head: environment
name: Coefficient strata and original divisors

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $C=A^TB$. Expanding $z^TCz$ shows that $Q\equiv0$ exactly when
$C+C^T=0$. Every skew $2\times2$ matrix is $\lambda J$, of rank zero
if $\lambda=0$ and rank two otherwise. If a matrix has rank zero the
composition vanishes. If the coefficient ranks are $(1,2)$ or $(2,1)$,
$C$ has rank one, so its quadratic form is nonzero. In the $(1,1)$ case
write $A=u\alpha_c^T$, $B=v\beta_c^T$; then
\[
 C=\alpha_c(u^Tv)\beta_c^T,\qquad
 Q=(u^Tv)(\alpha_c^Tz)(\beta_c^Tz).
\]
Since the polynomial ring has no zero divisors, $Q=0$ precisely when
$u^Tv=0$. If both ranks are two, $C$ is invertible and can be skew or
have a nonzero symmetric part. This proves exhaustion, and the table
proves nonemptiness. The seven impossible triples are the five zero-rank
pairs with $\epsilon=1$, together with $(1,2,0)$ and $(2,1,0)$.

For $a=2,b=1$, factor the actual matrix $B=v\beta_c^T$ with nonzero
vectors. The nonzero section $\sigma=\beta_c^Tz$ has one simple zero
$p$, so $\psi=v\sigma$ is sheaf-injective and has image $L(-p)$; its
fiber map does vanish at $p$. Also
$\phi|_L=(A^Tv)^Tz\ne0$, since $A$ is invertible. This section of
$\operatorname{Hom}(L,E_0)=\mathcal O(1)$ has one simple zero $q_0$.
Their product is nonzero with divisor $p+q_0$. For any prescribed
$p,q_0$, choose nonzero linear sections $\sigma,\tau$ with those
divisors and put
$v=(A^T)^{-1}\operatorname{coeff}(\tau)$,
$B=v\operatorname{coeff}(\sigma)^T$. Thus no ordered pair is omitted.
For $A=I$, $v=e_0$, $\sigma=z_0$ gives $p=q_0=[0:1]$, while
$\sigma=z_1$ gives $p=[1:0]\ne q_0=[0:1]$.
Inverse scalar rescaling of $v,\sigma$ does not alter the original map
or the divisors. No metric splitting along $L$ or base change is used.

Repeated primary roots also remain: $A=I$ and
$B=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ have
both ranks two and $Q=z_0^2$.

label: geo-metric-covariance
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{geo-metric-covariance}
An allowed holomorphic chain isomorphism gives a bijection of all smooth
positive metric triples, preserves the ordered equation and strict
calibration, and also intertwines the invariant equation on $\mathcal X$.
head: environment
name: Metric covariance

title: Proof
body_md:
Transport metrics by
$h'_j=(g_j^{-1})^*h_jg_j^{-1}$, with inverse
$h_j=g_j^*h'_jg_j$. Then $g_j:(E_j,h_j)\to(E_j,h'_j)$ is an isometry.
For an arrow $\Phi:E_s\to E_t$,
\[
 \Phi'=g_t\Phi g_s^{-1},\qquad
 (\Phi')^{\dagger_{h'}}=g_s\Phi^{\dagger_h}g_t^{-1}.
\]
Hence each of $P_1,R_1,P_2,R_2$ is conjugated at its own vertex. The
Chern connections and curvatures obey
\[
 D'_j=g_jD_jg_j^{-1},\quad F'_j=g_jF_jg_j^{-1},\quad
 H'_j=g_jH_jg_j^{-1},\quad
 \xi'_i=g_{i-1}\xi_i g_i^{-1}.
\]
The last formula follows by applying the transported source and target
connections; their derivative terms cancel. The allowed automorphisms
are constant, so no local $\partial g_j$ term is needed. Wedge
composition and metric adjoints give
\[
 K'_j=g_jK_jg_j^{-1},\quad S'_j=g_jS_jg_j^{-1},\quad
 \mathcal A'_j=g_j\mathcal A_jg_j^{-1},\quad
 \mathcal B'_j=g_j\mathcal B_jg_j^{-1}.
\]
In particular the entire anticommutator is conjugated, with no change in
order. The calibration is also conjugated, and for $w'\ne0$,
\[
 h'_j(\mathcal C'_jw',w')
 =h_j(\mathcal C_jg_j^{-1}w',g_j^{-1}w').
\]
This proves positivity in the transported metric.
The induced $\widetilde g=\bigoplus_jp_1^*g_j\otimes I_{\mathcal O(2j)}$
intertwines \eqref{geo-dolbeault}, commutes with the vertical $SU(2)$
action, and fixes the K\"ahler form. It conjugates $F_D$ and
$(\widetilde\omega I-F_D)^2$, including their Hermitian real and imaginary
parts, proving invariant transfer of the equation and calibration.
head: environment

label: geo-bridge
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{geo-bridge}
Restriction from $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ to $SU(2)$ gives a bijection on coherent
equivariant subobjects of every bundle \eqref{geo-dolbeault}. The underlying
image sheaf, monomorphism, quotient, nonsaturation, and nonreduced structure
are preserved.
head: environment
name: Compact and complex equivariant subobjects

title: Proof
body_md:
An equivariant monomorphism is determined by its invariant image
$\mathcal S\subset\mathcal E$: injectivity forces its linearization to
be the restricted one. An invariant image and its quotient inherit their
linearizations. It is therefore enough to extend invariance of
$\mathcal S$ from $K=SU(2)$ to its complexification $G=SL_2(\mathbb C)$.

For $\xi\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$, consider $\exp(z\xi)$, $z\in\mathbb C$.
Since $\mathcal X$ is projective, GAGA
\cite[\S12, Theorems 2--3]{SerreGAGA} places the coherent quotient
$q:\mathcal E\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal E/\mathcal S$ at a point of the
projective Quot scheme with its Hilbert polynomial, by Grothendieck's
construction \cite[Theorem 5.1]{NitsureQuot}. The given
$G$-linearization induces a holomorphic action on this scheme. The orbit
map $z\mapsto\exp(z\xi)\cdot[q]$ is constant on the real axis by
$K$-invariance. The holomorphic identity theorem, applied in local
coordinates and then using separatedness, makes it constant on
$\mathbb C$. Equality of Quot points gives equality of kernels. Thus
$\mathcal S$ is invariant under $\exp(i\xi)$ for every $\xi$.
Polar decomposition $G=K\exp(i\mathfrak{su}(2))$ proves $G$-invariance.
The inherited $G$-linearization is unique and gives the quotient
linearization in the unchanged exact coherent sequence. No saturation or
local freeness on the surface was required.

One can also see the extension in a finite-dimensional representation.
Take the naturally linearized ample bundle
$L_a=p_1^*\mathcal O(1)\otimes p_2^*\mathcal O(1)$. For $n$ sufficiently
large, Serre global generation, as recalled in
\cite[\S2, Lemma 2.1(c)]{NitsureQuot}, gives
\[
 W=H^0(\mathcal X,\mathcal S\otimes L_a^n)
       \subset H^0(\mathcal X,\mathcal E\otimes L_a^n)=V.
\]
This is a $K$-invariant complex subspace of a finite-dimensional
holomorphic $G$-representation. Differentiating real one-parameter
invariance gives $d\rho(\xi)W\subset W$; complex linearity gives
$d\rho(i\xi)W\subset W$. Polar decomposition then makes $W$
$G$-invariant. The equivariant evaluation map
$W\otimes L_a^{-n}\to\mathcal E$ has image exactly $\mathcal S$.
Both arguments preserve all finite-support quotient data and apply to
every boundary map, whose induced linearization is unchanged.
head: environment

label: geo-torsion
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Every quotient has positive imaginary charge

label: geo-subobject-charge
title: Proof
body_md:
The charge computation above, applied to coherent filtration quotients,
gives
\begin{equation}\label{geo-subobject-charge}
 Z(S)=2(A_Z+iB_Z),\qquad
 A_Z=\rho_0+\rho_1+\rho_2-e_1-2e_2,\qquad
 B_Z=e_0+e_1+e_2+\rho_1+2\rho_2.
\end{equation}
For the ambient chain these numbers are $(-2,12)$. The component bounds
are $e_0\le3$, $e_2\le1$, and $e_1\le2$ or $4$ according as its rank is
one or two. Omitting any ambient rank reduces the maximum $B_Z$ from
$3+6+3=12$ to at most $9$. For full ranks, put
$e_0=3-\ell_0$, $e_1=4-\ell_1$, $e_2=1-\ell_2$; then
$B_Z=12-\ell_0-\ell_1-\ell_2$. Equality forces all quotient lengths
zero and the entire chain. Thus every proper subchain has $B_Z<12$ and
every nonzero quotient has
$\operatorname{Im}Z(\mathcal E/S)=2(12-B_Z)>0$.
This argument includes arbitrary finite-colength and nonreduced quotients.
head: environment

label: geo-algebraic-classification
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{geo-algebraic-classification}
For every original coefficient pair, equivariant stability,
semistability and polystability coincide, and hold exactly when
$a=2$, $b>0$, $Q\not\equiv0$.
head: environment
name: Equivariant algebraic classification

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first these three conditions. The complete rank list is the first
row of \eqref{geo-all-patterns}, with $K_A=\mathcal O(1)$. If the pattern
is $010$, then $S_1\subset K_A$ and $e_1\le1$. For $110$ either the
same inclusion holds, or the nonzero upper restriction gives $e_0\ge e_1$.
For $120$, surjectivity of $\phi$ induces a surjection
$E_1/S_1\twoheadrightarrow E_0/S_0$; hence
$\ell_0\le\ell_1$, or $e_0\ge e_1-1$. In pattern $111$ both restrictions
are nonzero, so $e_0\ge e_1\ge e_2$, $e_2\le1$ and $e_1\le2$.
If $b=2$ its middle saturation is $\mathcal O(1)$ and $e_1\le1$; if
$b=1$ the saturation is $M_B=\mathcal O(2)$, retaining the length-one
torsion between $\operatorname{im}\psi$ and $M_B$. For $121$ the same
upper quotient surjection gives $\ell_0\le\ell_1$.

For $B_Z>0$, these actual incidences give the following bounds:
\begin{equation}\label{geo-strict-bounds}
\begin{array}{c|l|c}
 \rho&\text{incidence or admitted-charge condition}&F(S)\\\hline
 100&e_0>0&e_0+6\ge7\\
 010&e_1\le1&7-5e_1\ge2\\
 110, S_1\subset K_A&e_1\le1, e_0\ge-e_1&F\ge13-6e_1\ge7\\
 110, S_1\not\subset K_A&e_0\ge e_1, e_1\le2&F\ge13-4e_1\ge5\\
 120&e_0\ge e_1-1, e_1\le4&F\ge19-4e_1\ge3\\
 111&e_0\ge e_1\ge e_2, e_1\le2, e_2\le1&F\ge2\\
 121&\ell_0\le\ell_1&F=-\ell_0+5\ell_1+11\ell_2>0.
\end{array}
\end{equation}
For $111$, the estimate is $F\ge21-4e_1-11e_2\ge2$.
For proper $121$, $F\ge4\ell_1+11\ell_2$; equality would give
$\ell_0=\ell_1=\ell_2=0$ and the whole chain.

The admitted negative real axis has not been omitted. If $B_Z=0$, the
same incidences give $A_Z>0$: for $100,010$ it is respectively $1,2$;
for the killed $110$ case $A_Z=2-e_1\ge1$, and otherwise
$e_0=-e_1-1\ge e_1$ forces $e_1\le-1$. In $120$,
$e_0=-e_1-2\ge e_1-1$ forces $e_1\le-1$, so $A_Z\ge4$.
For $111$, $e_0+e_1+e_2=-3$ and $e_0\ge e_2$ imply
$e_1+2e_2\le-3$, hence $A_Z\ge6$. For $121$,
$\ell_0+\ell_1+\ell_2=12$ and $\ell_0\le\ell_1$ imply
$\ell_1+\ell_2\ge6$, so $A_Z=-2+\ell_1+2\ell_2\ge4$.
None of these charges is negative real. Lemma~\ref{geo-torsion} and
\eqref{geo-strict-bounds} prove stability, including every middle
embedding and nonsaturated modification.

Every other coefficient stratum has the following strict destabilizer:
\begin{equation}\label{geo-destabilizers}
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 \text{condition}&S&(A_Z,B_Z)&F(S)\\\hline
 a=0&(0,E_1,0)&(-2,6)&-6\\
 a=1&(0,K_A,0),\ K_A=\mathcal O(2)&(-1,3)&-3\\
 a=2, b=0&(0,0,E_2)&(-1,3)&-3\\
 (a,b,\epsilon)=(2,2,0)&(0,K_A,E_2)&(-1,5)&-1.
\end{array}
\end{equation}
In the last row $\operatorname{im}\psi=\ker\phi=\mathcal O(1)$,
so it is a legal subchain. Each charge has positive imaginary part and
phase strictly above $\theta_4$. The eleven-stratum exhaustion in
Lemma~\ref{geo-domain} shows that these rows cover every other pair.
They exclude semistability. A stable object is polystable through its
one-summand decomposition; conversely the definition of polystability
includes semistability. The three loci therefore coincide.
head: environment

label: geo-lyapunov
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{geo-lyapunov}
At a solution of \eqref{geo-equation}, put
$T_j=\chi I+\eta S_j$ and $L_j=\chi I+\eta H_j$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{geo-two-lyapunov}
 \tfrac12\{T_j,\mathcal C_j\}=I+S_j^2+K_j>0,\qquad
 \tfrac12\{T_j,L_j\}=I+\eta^2K_j>0,
 \qquad T_j>0,\quad L_j>0.
\end{equation}
The metric-linearized principal symbol is, up to the common curvature
sign, $g^{z\bar z}\zeta_z\bar\zeta_z\{T_j,u_j\}/2$ at each vertex.
Every strictly calibrated solution is therefore positively strongly
elliptic.
head: environment
name: Lyapunov identities and the symbol

title: Proof
body_md:
The phase equation gives $\mathcal A_j=\chi\mathcal C_j$ and
$\mathcal B_j=\eta\mathcal C_j$. Substitute these into
\eqref{geo-AB}, retaining both orders of $H_jS_j$; this gives the two
identities in \eqref{geo-two-lyapunov}. Testing the first on an eigenvector
of the Hermitian $T_j$ shows that each eigenvalue is positive because
$\mathcal C_j>0$. The second then gives positivity of $L_j$ by the
inverse Lyapunov formula
\[
 L_j=2\int_0^\infty e^{-tT_j}(I+\eta^2K_j)e^{-tT_j}\,dt.
\]
For a metric variation $h_j(t)(v,w)=h_j(e^{tu_j}v,w)$,
$u_j=u_j^\dagger$, the curvature convention gives
$\dot H_j=-g^{z\bar z}\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}u_j$ plus lower-order
terms. Adjoint and $S_j$ variations are zero order; derivative and
$K_j$ variations are at most first order. Thus the second-order part of
$\chi\mathcal B_j-\eta\mathcal A_j$ is
$\{T_j,\dot H_j\}/2$. If the eigenvalues of $T_j$ are $t_a$, its
matrix-entry multipliers are $(t_a+t_b)/2$. Ellipticity is equivalent
to absence of zero pair sums; positive strong ellipticity is equivalent
to $T_j>0$. The identity at an actual calibrated solution supplies that
positivity. Calibration alone away from the equation need not do so.
This is a symbol statement, rather than a global-kernel or inverse theorem.
head: environment

label: geo-elementary-exclusions
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Elementary all-metric exclusions

title: Proof
body_md:
When the upper coefficient rank is at most one, its two linear components
have a common zero, including the identically zero case. At this point
$P_1=S_0=0$ and $T_0=\chi I<0$, contradicting
Lemma~\ref{geo-lyapunov}. If $B=0$, then $R_2=K_2=0$ and $S_2=2I$.
The scalar bottom equation is
$-(H_2+2)=6(1-2H_2)$, so $H_2=8/11$ everywhere. Its integral is
$16\pi/11$, whereas Chern--Weil on $E_2=\mathcal O(1)$ gives $2\pi$.
This second contradiction does not require calibration. Both arguments
apply to every smooth positive metric triple.
head: environment

label: geo-euler-exclusion
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Euler-sequence all-metric exclusion

label: geo-euler-products
title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose such a solution exists. Full pointwise rank and zero composition
give the actual holomorphic Euler sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow I_b:=\operatorname{im}\psi=\ker\phi\simeq\mathcal O(1)
 \longrightarrow E_1\longrightarrow\mathcal Q\simeq\mathcal O(3)
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
Let $P$ be the actual $h_1$-orthogonal projection onto $I_b$ and
$P^\perp=I-P$. For smooth positive functions $x,y$ the rank-one arrow
products are
\begin{equation}\label{geo-euler-products}
 P_1=xI_{E_0},\quad R_1=xP^\perp,\qquad
 P_2=yP,\quad R_2=yI_{E_2}.
\end{equation}
Thus $S_1=(1+y)P+(1-x)P^\perp$. The quotient eigenvalue of $T_1$ is
$(5-6x)/\sqrt{37}$, so its positivity implies
\begin{equation}\label{geo-euler-x}
 0<x<5/6.
\end{equation}
This is the metric-orthogonal splitting, not a holomorphic splitting or
an assumption that $H_1$ preserves $I_b$.

Let $\beta=P^\perp D_1^{1,0}P|_{I_b}$ be the second fundamental form.
The Chern connection in this smooth splitting is
\[
 D_1=\begin{pmatrix}D_{I_b}&-\beta^\dagger\\
                         \beta&D_{\mathcal Q}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Gauss--Codazzi in the fixed curvature convention
\cite[Ch.~V, \S14, equations (14.6)--(14.7)]{Demailly2012} gives
$P^\perp H_1P^\perp=H_{\mathcal Q}-\beta\beta^\dagger$, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{geo-euler-gauss}
 \int_X\operatorname{tr}(P^\perp H_1)\omega_X
       =6\pi-\int_X|\beta|^2\omega_X.
\end{equation}
Differentiating $\phi P=0$ and $P^\perp\psi=0$ yields
$\xi_1P=-\phi\beta$ and $P^\perp\xi_2=\beta\psi$. By
\eqref{geo-euler-products},
\begin{equation}\label{geo-euler-derivatives}
 |\xi_1P|^2=x|\beta|^2,\qquad
 |P^\perp\xi_2|^2=y|\beta|^2.
\end{equation}

Set $V=2\pi$, $\ell_Q=\operatorname{tr}(P^\perp L_1)$ and
$k_Q=\operatorname{tr}(P^\perp K_1)$. The upper identity in
\eqref{geo-endpoint-integrals}, with $R_1=xP^\perp$, is
\begin{equation}\label{geo-euler-top}
 \frac{9V}{\sqrt{37}}
       =\int_Xx\ell_Q\omega_X+\frac\eta2\int_X|\xi_1|^2\omega_X.
\end{equation}
Project the second identity of \eqref{geo-two-lyapunov} at vertex one
onto $P^\perp$. Although $L_1$ need not preserve the splitting, $T_1$
does; cyclicity of trace gives
\begin{equation}\label{geo-euler-middle}
 [\chi+\eta(1-x)]\ell_Q=1+\eta^2k_Q,\qquad
 x\ell_Q=\tfrac56\ell_Q-\tfrac1\eta-\eta k_Q.
\end{equation}
Both kinetic halves are retained:
\begin{equation}\label{geo-euler-kinetics}
 k_Q=\tfrac12\bigl(|\xi_1P^\perp|^2+|P^\perp\xi_2|^2\bigr),\qquad
 \int_X\ell_Q\omega_X
       =\frac{17V-6\int_X|\beta|^2\omega_X}{\sqrt{37}},
\end{equation}
where the last identity uses \eqref{geo-euler-gauss} and
$L_1=\chi I+\eta H_1$.

Substitute \eqref{geo-euler-middle} and \eqref{geo-euler-kinetics} into
\eqref{geo-euler-top}, splitting
$|\xi_1|^2=|\xi_1P|^2+|\xi_1P^\perp|^2$. The quotient half of the
upper derivative cancels its actual half in $k_Q$. The remaining equality
is
\[
 9V=8V-5\int_X|\beta|^2\omega_X
           +3\int_X|\xi_1P|^2\omega_X
           -3\int_X|P^\perp\xi_2|^2\omega_X.
\]
Using \eqref{geo-euler-derivatives} gives
\begin{equation}\label{geo-euler-contradiction}
 2\pi=\int_X(3x-3y-5)|\beta|^2\omega_X.
\end{equation}
Since $x<5/6$ and $y>0$, the coefficient is strictly less than $-5/2$.
The right side is nonpositive, also when $\beta=0$, while the left side
is positive. This excludes arbitrary metric triples, without a
representative normalization or base automorphism.
head: environment

label: geo-main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{geo-main}
For every $A,B\in\operatorname{Mat}_2(\mathbb C)$, on the fixed original
chain and background of \eqref{geo-chain}, the following are equivalent:
\begin{align*}
 &\mathrm{Ex}(A,B),\\
 &\mathcal E_{A,B}\text{ is }SU(2)\text{-equivariantly }Z\text{-stable},\\
 &\mathcal E_{A,B}\text{ is }SU(2)\text{-equivariantly }Z\text{-semistable},\\
 &\mathcal E_{A,B}\text{ is }SU(2)\text{-equivariantly }Z\text{-polystable},\\
 &\operatorname{rank}A=2\quad\text{and}\quad Q\not\equiv0.
\end{align*}
Thus all three stability predicates and smooth strictly calibrated
existence hold on $(2,1,1)$ and $(2,2,1)$, and fail on each of the nine
other nonempty triples of Lemma~\ref{geo-domain}. In particular there
are no strictly semistable objects in this fixed family.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The algebraic result, Proposition~\ref{geo-algebraic-classification}, was
proved solely from the coherent equivalence, the compact-to-complex
bridge, charge, full subobject inventory and phase inequalities.
Since $Q\not\equiv0$ implies $B\ne0$, it identifies all three predicates
with $\operatorname{rank}A=2$, $Q\not\equiv0$.

We establish the analytic criterion on the same original inputs. If
$\operatorname{rank}A=2$, $Q\not\equiv0$, then $B$ has rank one or two.
In rank two this is exactly the full primary family; the original-chain
existence theorem \ref{primary-existence} applies, including repeated
composition roots. In rank one, Lemma~\ref{geo-domain} factors the actual
map as $v\sigma$ with saturation $\mathcal O(2)v$, its lower zero $p$,
and upper restriction divisor $q_0$. Both $p=q_0$ and $p\ne q_0$ belong
to the original-chain existence theorem \ref{lower-existence}. Hence a
smooth strictly calibrated metric triple exists for every pair in
either stratum.

Conversely, if such a metric triple exists,
Proposition~\ref{geo-elementary-exclusions} forces
$\operatorname{rank}A=2$ and $B\ne0$. If $Q$ vanished identically,
rank-one $B$ would be impossible by its actual factorization in
Lemma~\ref{geo-domain}. Rank-two $B$ would give $(2,2,0)$, excluded by
Proposition~\ref{geo-euler-exclusion}. Thus $Q\not\equiv0$.
This proves the analytic equivalence independently of stability; joining
the two same-input equivalences proves the theorem and every boundary
row. The eight low-rank or zero-lower triples are excluded by the first
proposition and the remaining composition-zero triple by the second.
head: environment

label: common-fields
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{common-fields}
After the fixed \(G\)-conjugation, use the real bundle
\(\mathscr H=\mathbb R\oplus\operatorname{Herm}_2\oplus\mathbb R\), with
inner product
\(aa'+\operatorname{tr}(MM')+bb'\).  Every positive metric triple has
unique reference-selfadjoint logarithmic variables \(w=(a,M,b)\):
\[
 h(w)=h_*e^w,\qquad f=e^M,\quad S=e^{M/2}.
\]
Square-root transport defines
\(\widehat F_j(w)=e^{w_j/2}F_j(h(w))e^{-w_j/2}\).  The transported
arrow products and symbols are
\begin{equation}\label{common-symbols}
 \begin{gathered}
 R=e^aS^{-1}R_*S^{-1},\qquad P=e^{-b}SP_*S,
 \qquad p=\operatorname{tr}R,\quad r=\operatorname{tr}P,\\
 q=p-\alpha,\qquad \beta=d-r,\qquad V=cI-R+P,\qquad
 \mathcal L_VH=\tfrac12(VH+HV).
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The legal domain is \(q>0,\ \beta>0,\ V>0\).  Put
\[
 B(w)w=(qa,\mathcal L_VM,\beta b),\qquad
 v(w)=qa+\operatorname{tr}(VM)+\beta b.
\]
For one fixed prospective mass \(\mu_s>0\), the auxiliary equation is
\begin{equation}\label{common-auxiliary}
 \widehat F(w)+\tau\mu_s B(w)w=\tau F_*,
 \qquad 0<\tau\le1.
\end{equation}
Write its auxiliary residual as
\[
 \mathcal E(\tau,w)=\widehat F(w)+\tau\mu_sB(w)w-\tau F_*.
\]
Thus the auxiliary equation is exactly \(\mathcal E(\tau,w)=0\).
With \(t=\tau\mu_s\), its full rows are
\begin{equation}\label{common-positive-rows}
 \begin{aligned}
 H_0&=\alpha-ta+(C_0^\tau+K_0)/q,\\
 \widehat H_1&=\alpha I-tM+\mathcal L_V^{-1}(C_1^\tau+K_1),\\
 H_2&=\alpha-tb+(C_2^\tau+K_2)/\beta,
 \end{aligned}\qquad C_1^\tau=A_0I+\tau F_{*,1}.
\end{equation}
All variables are unrestricted real scalars or full Hermitian matrices.
head: environment
name: Metric variables and auxiliary equation

label: common-normalization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{common-normalization}
The total residual integral vanishes for every metric triple.  Every exact
positive-parameter solution satisfies \(N(w):=\int_Xv(w)\omega_X=0\).
There is precisely one common constant to remove in the reference chart.
head: environment
name: The single constant normalization

label: common-total-trace
title: Proof
body_md:
The actual arrow Bochner identities are
\[
 \Delta p=2K_0-pH_0+\operatorname{tr}(R\widehat H_1),\qquad
 \Delta r=2K_2-\operatorname{tr}(P\widehat H_1)+rH_2,
 \qquad\operatorname{tr}K_1=K_0+K_2.
\]
Substitution into the residual gives
\begin{equation}\label{common-total-trace}
 \operatorname{tr}_{\rm tot}\widehat F
 =-\alpha H_0+c\operatorname{tr}\widehat H_1+dH_2
   -\Delta(p+r)-\frac{14}{3}.
\end{equation}
Here \(q+\operatorname{tr}V+\beta=W\), and
\(\alpha W+4A_0=14/3\).  The degrees \((3,4,1)\) imply that its integral
is \((-3\alpha+4c+d-14/3)\operatorname{Vol}(X)=0\).
Transport preserves trace.  Integrating \eqref{common-auxiliary} gives
\(tN(w)=0\), hence the assertion for \(t>0\).

For \(T(k)=(k,kI,k)\), common constant translation leaves the arrows,
curvature, residual and symbols unchanged and
\(N(w+T(k))=N(w)+kW\operatorname{Vol}(X)\).  Let
\[
 A_*U=(q_*a,\mathcal L_{V_*}M,\beta_*b),\quad
 L_0(U)=\int_X\operatorname{tr}_{\rm tot}(A_*U)\omega_X,
 \quad X'=\ker L_0,
\]
and let \(Y\) be the space of sources of zero total integral.  Then
\[
 \mathcal P(u)=u-T\!\left(\frac{N(u)}{W\operatorname{Vol}(X)}\right)
\]
maps \(X'\) bijectively to \(N=0\), with inverse
\(w\mapsto w-T(L_0(w)/(W\operatorname{Vol}(X)))\).  Moreover
\(D\mathcal P(0)|_{X'}=I\), since \(DN(0)=L_0\).  These are closed
codimension-one spaces.  No nonconstant scalar, relative scalar, or matrix
direction is removed, and no separate vertex mean is imposed.
head: environment

label: common-trace-comparison
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{common-trace-comparison}
For every finite field, not merely for solutions, put
\[
 T=-\alpha a+c\operatorname{tr}M+db+p+r-p_*-r_*(x),\qquad
 v=qa+\operatorname{tr}(VM)+\beta b.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{common-radial-inequalities}
 T\ge q_*a+\operatorname{tr}(V_*M)+\beta_*b,
 \qquad v\ge T.
\end{equation}
Every auxiliary solution satisfies the exact scalar equation
\begin{equation}\label{common-trace-equation}
 \Delta T=(1-\tau)f_*+tv,\qquad
 f_*=\operatorname{tr}_{\rm tot}F_* ,\quad t=\tau\mu.
\end{equation}
These statements allow semidefinite \(P_*\), including \(P_*(x)=0\).
head: environment
name: The radial trace comparison

title: Proof
body_md:
Cyclic trace, without commuting the two arrows, gives along the radial field
\[
 p(sw)=\operatorname{tr}(R_*e^{s(aI-M)}),\qquad
 r(sw)=\operatorname{tr}(P_*e^{s(M-bI)}).
\]
The spectral inequality \(e^A\ge I+A\), paired with the fixed positive
semidefinite weights, proves the first inequality.  The scalar function
\(k(y)=ye^y-e^y+1\) is nonnegative: its derivative is \(ye^y\) and its
unique minimum is zero at the origin.  Spectral calculus therefore gives
\[
 v-T=\operatorname{tr}(R_*k(aI-M))+
       \operatorname{tr}(P_*k(M-bI))\ge0.
\]
Neither calculation assumes that intermediate radial fields have positive
symbols.  Substitution of the full trace identity from
Lemma~\ref{common-normalization}, with
\(\operatorname{tr}\widehat H_1=4-\Delta\operatorname{tr}M\), proves
\eqref{common-trace-equation}.  The variable baseline \(r_*(x)\) is kept;
its derivatives are part of \(f_*\).
head: environment

label: common-positive-size
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{common-positive-size}
For every actual positive-symbol solution with \(0<\tau\le1\) and
\(C_1^\tau\ge0\),
\begin{equation}\label{common-size-estimate}
 t\max(\|a\|_\infty,\|b\|_\infty,\|M\|_{\infty,\mathrm{op}})
 \le C_{\rm size}.
\end{equation}
The constant depends only on the fixed reference and background, not on
\(\mu,\tau\), a symbol minimum, or the existence of any other solution.
For the primary reference this is the primary estimate; for the boundary
reference it is a separate estimate with recomputed fixed-data constants.
head: environment
name: Independent positive-parameter size estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
Set \(C_L=\sup(H_{*0}-\alpha)=d+\max n_\phi\) and
\(F_T=\|f_*\|_\infty\).  At a minimum of \(a\),
\(H_0\le H_{*0}\); the positive top source in
\eqref{common-positive-rows} gives \(a\ge-C_L/t\).  At a minimum of
\(b\), the bottom row similarly gives \(b\ge-c/t\).
Let \(m=\min_X\lambda_{\min}M\), and take a constant reference-unit
vector \(e\) at an attaining eigenline.  The globally defined function
\(e^*f^{-1}e\) has its maximum there, also for repeated spectra.  Direct
ordered differentiation yields at that point
\[
 \Delta(e^*f^{-1}e)
 =e^{-m}(e^*\widehat H_1e-2)
 +g^{-1}e^{-2m}e^*f_zf^{-1}f_{\bar z}e.
\]
The last term is nonnegative, so \(\widehat H_{1,ee}\le2\).
The positive Lyapunov inverse in \eqref{common-lyapunov-inverse} gives
\(\widehat H_1\ge\alpha I-tM\), hence \(m\ge-d/t\).
This argument needs semipositive middle force, not a positive lower-arrow
norm or a uniform inverse bound.

At a maximum of \(T\), \eqref{common-trace-equation} and \(v\ge T\)
give \(T\le F_T/t\).  The shifted fields
\(a+C_L/t,b+C_L/t,M+(C_L/t)I\) are nonnegative.  The reference weights
are at least \(\delta=4/21\), and their sum is \(W\).  Thus
\[
 \delta\bigl(a+C_L/t+\operatorname{tr}(M+(C_L/t)I)+b+C_L/t\bigr)
 \le (F_T+C_LW)/t.
\]
For example \(C_{\rm size}=\max(C_L,(F_T+C_LW)/\delta)\) suffices.
Only semidefiniteness of \(P_*\) was used, so the boundary proof applies
at its zero as well.  No normalization premise was needed: an exact
positive-parameter solution is normalized by its total integral.
head: environment

label: common-positive-energy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{common-positive-energy}
In the primary setting, fix \(\tau_->0\), a finite \(\mu\), and a closed
interval \([\tau_-,T_+]\) with \(C_1^\tau\ge c_1I>0\).
There are fixed-stage constants \(B,E_B\) for all solutions such that
\[
 |a|,|b|,\|M\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le B,\qquad
 \int_X(|DM|^2+K_0+K_2+\operatorname{tr}V^{-1})\,\omega_X\le E_B.
\]
These constants are not asserted uniform as \(\tau_-\downarrow0\).
head: environment
name: Positive-stage integral estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
The preceding lemma already gives the required \(B\).  The independent
entropy route behind the same stage estimate can also be recorded without
any symbol buffer.  Put \(C=C_L/(\tau_-\mu)\),
\(\lambda=\lambda_{\max}M\), and \(E=\log(112/27)\).
The top norm gives \(a\le\lambda+E\).  If \(m_i\) are the eigenvalues
of \(M\), and \(c_i\) the spectral weights of its reference top unit
vector, let \(d_i=c_ie^{-m_i}/\sum c_je^{-m_j}\), omitting zero
supports.  The relative entropy \(D_- =\sum d_i\log(d_i/c_i)\ge0\)
follows from \(\log x\le x-1\), and expansion gives
\[
 a-\operatorname{tr}(RM)/p=\log(p/p_*)+D_-.
\]
Together with the lower bounds, \(r+\beta=d\), and
\(p\log(p/p_*)\ge-p_*/e\), this implies
\[
 v\ge \tfrac23\lambda_++\beta b_+-K,
 \qquad K=CW+\alpha E+p_*/e.
\]
Normalization gives \(\int\lambda_+\le(3/2)K\operatorname{Vol}X\)
and \(\int\beta b_+\le K\operatorname{Vol}X\).
If \(\beta<d/2\), then
\(r\le r_{*,\max}e^{\lambda-b}\) and \(r>d/2\) imply \(b<\lambda\);
otherwise \(b_+\le(2/d)\beta b_+\).  These facts and
\(\operatorname{tr}M_+\le2\lambda_+\) bound the unweighted
\(L^1\) norm of all six fields.  The trace equation then has
\(\Delta T\ge-D_0\) and \(\int|T|\le A\), with fixed-stage constants.
The actual chordal Green identity \eqref{common-green-kernel} gives
\(T\le m_\omega A/(2\pi)+n_\omega D_0\), where
\(m_\omega=\sup\omega_{\rm FS}/\omega_X\) and
\(n_\omega=\sup\omega_X/\omega_{\rm FS}\).
Finally
\(-\alpha a+c\operatorname{tr}M+db
 \ge(2/3)\lambda-(c+d)C-\alpha E\)
recovers all upper values.  This argument uses no weighted trace with an
assumed \(V\)-gap.

For the integral assertion differentiate \(h=f^{-1}\) in its actual
order.  The middle row is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{common-inverse-trace-row}
 \Delta h=g^{-1}hf_zhf_{\bar z}h-dh-tMh
       +S^{-1}\mathcal L_V^{-1}(C_1^\tau+K_1)S^{-1}.
\end{equation}
On the proved value range the first trace term controls \(|DM|^2\):
the divided differences of \(D\exp_M\) lie between \(e^{-B}\) and
\(e^B\), including repeated spectra.  Moreover \(V\le(c+d)I\), and
trace self-adjointness gives
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}\mathcal L_V^{-1}(K_1)S^{-1})
 \ge \frac{e^{-B}}{c+d}(K_0+K_2),\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}\mathcal L_V^{-1}(C_1^\tau)S^{-1})
 \ge c_1e^{-B}\operatorname{tr}V^{-1}.
\]
The negative terms are bounded below by \(-2e^B(d+\mu B)\).
Thus, for a fixed \(a'_B>0\),
\(\Delta\operatorname{tr}h\ge a'_B(|DM|^2+K_0+K_2+
\operatorname{tr}V^{-1})-2e^B(d+\mu B)\).
Integration proves the claim.  This is an integral assertion only; the
pointwise gradients and gaps require the following full face argument.
head: environment

label: common-local-potentials
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{common-local-potentials}
The component Poisson and complex \(\bar\partial\) estimates used below
hold on nested coordinate disks.  A bounded two-sided Poisson source and
bounded values give compactness in \(C^1\), with gradient modulus
\(Ch(1+|\log h|)\).  A bounded complex function with bounded
\(\bar\partial\) source is locally precompact in \(C^\nu\) for every
\(\nu<1\).  A \(C^\gamma\) Poisson source gives a \(C^{2,\gamma}\)
solution.  A nonnegative entire distributionally superharmonic function
on the plane is constant.
head: environment
name: Local potential estimates

title: Proof
body_md:
For the Euclidean equation use
\(\Gamma(x)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|x|\) and a cutoff source; subtracting its
logarithmic potential leaves a distributionally harmonic function on a
smaller disk.  Mollification and radial mean values show this remainder
is smooth, and the circle formula bounds its interior derivatives by its
local value norm.  The gradient kernel is \(O(|x|^{-1})\).  Splitting the
difference of its integrals into disks of radius \(2h\) and their
complement gives \(Ch+Ch\int_{2h}^{R}dr/r\).  The same calculation with
the Cauchy kernel \(1/z\), and the holomorphic remainder's circle formula,
gives the stated \(\bar\partial\) compactness.

The Hessian kernel is
\[
 H_{ij}(x)=-\frac1{2\pi}
 \left(\frac{\delta_{ij}}{|x|^2}-\frac{2x_ix_j}{|x|^4}\right),
 \qquad
 \partial_i\partial_j\Gamma
 =\operatorname{pv}H_{ij}-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\delta_0.
\]
Its circular mean is zero.  Subtract the source value in the singular
integral.  The near integrand is bounded by
\(C[F]_\gamma |x|^{\gamma-2}\).  For two centers distance \(h\) apart,
the near contribution is \(O(h^\gamma)\); outside \(2h\), the kernel
difference is \(Ch|x|^{-3}\), giving
\(Ch[F]_\gamma\int_{2h}^Rr^{\gamma-2}dr=O(h^\gamma)\).
The constant-source kernel integral is uniformly bounded by circular
cancellation: a shifted excluded ball changes only an \(O(h)\)-annulus.
Cutoff terms are smooth.  This proves the Hessian estimate without a
logarithmic loss.

For the last assertion convolve the nonnegative superharmonic function
with a nonnegative smooth compactly supported probability kernel.  A
positive mass of its negative Laplacian in one disk makes its circular
mean derivative at most \(-m/(2\pi R)\) on every larger circle.
Integration in \(\log R\) contradicts nonnegativity.  Thus every
convolution is harmonic.  The differentiated Poisson formula bounds the
gradient of a nonnegative entire harmonic function at a center by its
value times \(C/R\).  Letting \(R\to\infty\) makes it constant, and
approximate identities give the distributional assertion.
head: environment

label: common-reference-inverse
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{common-reference-inverse}
For each of the two fixed-chain settings above and \(0<\gamma<1\), the
operator \(J_*+\mu A_*\), where \(J_*=D\widehat F(0)\), is an
isomorphism \(C^{2,\gamma}(X;\mathscr H)\to C^{0,\gamma}(X;\mathscr H)\)
for every sufficiently large finite \(\mu\).  It restricts to an
isomorphism \(X'\to Y\).
head: environment
name: Full nonsymmetric reference inverse

title: Proof
body_md:
The principal part is coercive, but the full linearization also has
coupled first-order terms and need not be symmetric. We keep those terms
in the calculation: a sufficiently large finite mass absorbs them in the
energy estimate, after which local elliptic estimates give the stated
inverse. The normalization is handled by restricting this unrestricted
inverse, rather than by dropping a scalar equation in advance.

The full ordered derivative is recorded explicitly to fix its lower-order
terms.  For \(U=(a,M,b)\), put \(Z=M-aI\), \(Y_0=M-bI\),
\(c_\phi=\phi Z\phi^*\), \(c_\psi=\psi^*Y_0\psi\).  All quantities in
this paragraph are at the fixed reference.  Square-root transport gives
\(J_*U=\dot F[U]+[U,F_*]/2\), including the off-shell commutator.
The changing-adjoint variations are
\[
 \dot q=-c_\phi,\quad\dot\beta=-c_\psi,\quad
 \dot V=\tfrac12(\{Z,R_*\}+\{Y_0,P_*\}),\quad
 \widehat{\dot\xi}=-\phi Z_z-\tfrac12\xi_*Z,\quad
 \widehat{\dot y}=Y_{0,z}\psi+\tfrac12Y_0y_*.
\]
Consequently
\begin{align*}
 \kappa_0&=-g^{-1}\operatorname{Re}(\phi Z_z\xi_*^*)
             -(2g)^{-1}\xi_*Z\xi_*^*,\\
 \kappa_2&=g^{-1}\operatorname{Re}(y_*^*Y_{0,z}\psi)
             +(2g)^{-1}y_*^*Y_0y_*,\\
 \mathcal K_1[U]&=-(2g)^{-1}
 (Z_{\bar z}\phi^*\xi_*+\xi_*^*\phi Z_z)
 -(4g)^{-1}\{Z,\xi_*^*\xi_*\}\\
 &\hspace{1em}+(2g)^{-1}
 (Y_{0,z}\psi y_*^*+y_*\psi^*Y_{0,\bar z})
 +(4g)^{-1}\{Y_0,y_*y_*^*\}.
\end{align*}
The curvature variations are \(-\Delta a,-\Delta M,-\Delta b\), because
the middle End connection is flat and its curvature is central.  The
resulting rows are
\begin{equation}\label{common-reference-linearization}
 \begin{aligned}
 (J_*U)_0&=-q_*\Delta a-(d+n_\phi)c_\phi-\kappa_0,\\
 (J_*U)_1&=-\mathcal L_{V_*}\Delta M
       +\tfrac d2(\{Z,R_*\}+\{Y_0,P_*\})-\mathcal K_1[U],\\
 (J_*U)_2&=-\beta_*\Delta b-c\,c_\psi-\kappa_2.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Thus \(J_*=-A_*\Delta+B_*D+C_*\), with smooth real coefficient
operators in all six directions.  In particular this is
\(-A_*\Delta\), not \(-\Delta(A_*\,\cdot)\).  The variable \(r_*(x)\)
contributes to \(DA_*\).  At a lower-arrow zero the terms involving
\(D\psi\) remain smooth; no norm reciprocal was used in this calculation.

Normalize the flat gradient by
\(-\int\langle U,\Delta U\rangle=\int|DU|^2\), and put
\[
 \delta=\frac4{21},\quad K=\|DA_*\|_\infty+\|B_*\|_\infty,
 \quad G_0=\|C_*\|_\infty+K^2/(2\delta),\quad
 \mu_0=(G_0+1)/\delta.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{tr}(V_*M^2)\ge\delta\operatorname{tr}(M^2)\),
\(A_*\ge\delta I\).  Integration by parts, including the derivative
of \(A_*\), and Young's inequality give for \(\mu\ge\mu_0\)
\begin{equation}\label{common-coercivity}
 \int_X\langle U,(J_*+\mu A_*)U\rangle\omega_X
 \ge\frac\delta2\|DU\|_2^2+\|U\|_2^2.
\end{equation}
No favorable sign is assigned to the coupled lower-order terms.

For completeness this also proves surjectivity, rather than only a
kernel assertion.  On the real Hilbert space \(H^1\) use the bounded form
\[
 b(U,Z)=\int\langle D(A_*Z),DU\rangle
       +\int\langle Z,B_*DU+C_*U+\mu A_*U\rangle.
\]
Its diagonal is bounded below by
\(c_H\|U\|_{H^1}^2\), \(c_H=\min(\delta/2,1)\).
The representing Hilbert operator is therefore bounded below and has
closed range.  A vector orthogonal to its range obeys \(b(U,Z)=0\) for
all \(U\); setting \(U=Z\) makes it zero.  Its range is also dense, hence
surjective.  Every \(L^2\) source has a unique weak \(H^1\) solution,
with norm at most \(c_H^{-1}\) times the source norm.  Neither this form
nor \(J_*\) is assumed symmetric.

Multiplication after the operator by the smooth \(A_*^{-1}\) gives scalar
principal part \(-\Delta\) with smooth coupled lower-order terms.
Initially the local Euclidean Poisson source is \(L^2\).  A cutoff
logarithmic potential has bounded values, and its gradient kernel is
locally \(L^s\) for \(s<2\).  For any finite \(p>2\), use
\(s=2p/(p+2)\) in convolution to obtain local \(W^{1,p}\).
The now \(L^p\) source gives \(C^{1,\nu}\),
\(\nu=1-2/p\), by the near/far gradient split.  Choose
\(p=4/(1-\gamma)\), so \(\nu=(1+\gamma)/2>\gamma\).  The source becomes
\(C^\gamma\), and the Hessian calculation of
Lemma~\ref{common-local-potentials} gives \(C^{2,\gamma}\).
A finite nested cover, including infinity, gives a norm bound by the
\(C^\gamma\) source and the initial \(H^1\) bound.  This proves the
unrestricted bounded inverse.

Differentiating the universal total integral gives
\(\int\operatorname{tr}_{\rm tot}J_*U=0\).  Hence
\[
 \int\operatorname{tr}_{\rm tot}(J_*+\mu A_*)U=\mu L_0(U).
\]
The full inverse sends \(Y\) into \(X'\), proving exactly the normalized
restriction without adding vertex conditions or an unproved cokernel
assumption.
head: environment

label: common-mass-inverse
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: A mass-uniform inverse

title: Proof
body_md:
Multiply after \(L_t\) by \(A_*^{-1}\).  The resulting operator is
\(-\Delta+\widetilde B D+\widetilde C+tI\), with smooth full coupled
lower coefficients.  In a holomorphic chart its scalar principal
coefficient is \(a(x)=1/(4g(x))\).  The fixed atlas gives a positive
compact range for \(a\); its coordinate weighted norms and \(N_t\) are
uniformly equivalent for \(t\ge1\).

For constant \(a>0\) in that range use the explicit Gaussian resolvent
\[
 H_{au}(x)=(4\pi au)^{-1}e^{-|x|^2/(4au)},\qquad
 R_t^aF=\int_0^\infty e^{-tu}H_{au}*F\,du.
\]
Differentiation and \(x=\sqrt u\,z\) give
\(\|D^kH_{au}\|_1\le C_ku^{-k/2}\) and, for \(k\ge1\),
\(\int|D^kH_{au}(x)||x|^\gamma dx\le C u^{(\gamma-k)/2}\).
Derivative kernels have integral zero.  Consequently
\[
 t\|R_t^aF\|_\gamma+\sqrt t\|DR_t^aF\|_\gamma
   +\|D^2R_t^aF\|_\gamma\le C\|F\|_\gamma,
 \qquad \|D^2R_t^aF\|_\infty\le C t^{-\gamma/2}[F]_\gamma.
\]
For the Hessian seminorm use cancellation for both two and three Gaussian
derivatives.  The difference at distance \(h\) is bounded by
\(C[F]_\gamma\min(u^{\gamma/2-1},h u^{(\gamma-3)/2})\).
Integrating separately over \((0,h^2)\) and \((h^2,\infty)\) gives
\(C[F]_\gamma h^\gamma\); both integrals converge for \(0<\gamma<1\).
The truncated resolvent satisfies
\((t-a\Delta_{\mathbb R^2})R_{t,\varepsilon}^aF
=e^{-t\varepsilon}H_{a\varepsilon}*F\).
As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), derivatives through order two converge
uniformly, the omitted Hessian integral being \(O(\varepsilon^{\gamma/2})\).
This proves the strong equation on big Hölder spaces.  No density of smooth
functions in their Hölder norm is asserted.

Refine the atlas by grids of a radius \(r\), with a partition \(\chi_j\),
cutoffs \(\psi_j=1\) on their supports, and centers \(x_j\).
The \(\psi_j\) supports have a fixed overlap bound, independent of \(r\),
and derivatives \(O(r^{-k})\).  With \(a_j=a(x_j)\), extend
\(\chi_jF\) by zero in its coordinate plane and put
\[
 S_tF=\sum_j\psi_jR_t^{a_j}(\chi_jF)_{\rm ext}.
\]
The cutoff product bound is
\(\|(\chi_jF)_{\rm ext}\|_\gamma\le Cr^{-\gamma}\|F\|_\gamma\).
For fixed \(r\), \(N_t(S_tF)\le K_r\|F\|_\gamma\).
Writing the full local operator as
\(-a\Delta_{\mathbb R^2}+b^k\partial_k+c_0+t\), its error on the
\(j\)-th summand is exactly
\begin{align*}
 E_{t,j}F={}&\psi_j(a_j-a)\Delta u_j
 +\psi_jb^k\partial_ku_j+\psi_jc_0u_j
 -2a\partial_k\psi_j\partial_ku_j\\
 &-a(\Delta\psi_j)u_j+(b^k\partial_k\psi_j)u_j,
 \qquad u_j=R_t^{a_j}(\chi_jF)_{\rm ext}.
\end{align*}
All but the first term are bounded by
\(C_r(t^{-1/2}+t^{-1})\|F\|_\gamma\).
For \(k_j=\psi_j(a_j-a)\),
\(\|k_j\|_\infty\le Cr\) and \([k_j]_\gamma\le Cr^{1-\gamma}\).
The split Hölder product estimate and the refined Hessian supremum bound
therefore give
\[
 \|k_j\Delta u_j\|_\gamma
 \le C\bigl(r^{1-\gamma}+r^{1-2\gamma}t^{-\gamma/2}\bigr)\|F\|_\gamma.
\]
At any pair of points only the supports containing one of the two points
contribute, at most twice the overlap bound.  The total patch count thus
does not multiply this estimate.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{common-parametrix-error}
 \|E_t\|\le C_0r^{1-\gamma}
      +C_r(t^{-\gamma/2}+t^{-1/2}+t^{-1}).
\end{equation}
Choose \(r\) first so that the first term is at most \(1/4\); keep it
fixed, and choose \(t_0\ge\max(1,\mu_0)\) so the remaining terms are at
most \(1/4\).  The series \((I+E_t)^{-1}=\sum_{m\ge0}(-E_t)^m\)
then has norm at most two.  It gives a strong six-field right inverse
\(S_t(I+E_t)^{-1}A_*^{-1}\), with the stated weighted bound.
The coercivity calculation \eqref{common-coercivity}, with \(\mu=t\),
proves injectivity.  This proves \eqref{common-weighted-inverse} with a
constant independent of \(t\).  The normalization restriction follows
as before from \(\int\operatorname{tr}_{\rm tot}L_tU=tL_0(U)\).
head: environment

label: common-gradient-gaps
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{common-gradient-gaps}
Fix either the primary reference or the separate lower-boundary reference,
a finite mass \(\mu\), and independently given \(B,c_1>0\).
In the primary setting the parameter range is \(0\le\tau\le1\).
In the lower-boundary setting it is the specified positive-force slab
\(0<\tau\le\tau_b\le T_+\), at the same fixed mass.
Every actual normalized solution in its stated range, with positive symbols,
\(|a|,|b|,\|M\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le B\), and \(C_1^\tau\ge c_1I\)
satisfies
\[
 \|Dw\|_\infty\le G_*,\qquad
 q\ge\delta_q>0,\quad\beta\ge\delta_\beta>0,\quad V\ge\delta_VI>0.
\]
The constants are uniform over this solution set, but depend on the fixed
setting, reference, background, \(B,c_1,\mu\).  No existence or value
estimate is part of the conclusion.
head: environment
name: The full gradient and gap estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof separates the gradient bound from the symbol gaps. A bounded
scalar potential first localizes the energy near a putative gradient
blow-up. On each boundary face, rescaling then forces a constant value
limit. To contradict blow-up, however, the argument must also preserve a
nonzero derivative at the rescaling center; the exact projected equations
and scalar transforms below provide that step, including both extreme
mixed ratios. Only after gradients are bounded do we estimate the gaps
at their separate global minima.

On bounded values, \((a,M,b)\) and \((a,f,b)\) have uniformly
equivalent first-derivative norms.  Set
\[
 \rho=\operatorname{tr}f^{-1},\quad U=\operatorname{tr}V^{-1},\quad
 W_1=\operatorname{tr}(V^{-1}K_1),\quad G_M=2\|M_z\|^2/g.
\]
The ordered identity \eqref{common-inverse-trace-row} gives
\[
 \Delta\rho\ge a_MG_M+e^{-B}W_1+c_1e^{-B}U-D_M,
 \qquad a_M=e^{-5B}/2.
\]
Write \(\Delta a=A_a-(C_0+K_0)/q\) and
\(\Delta b=A_b-(C_2+K_2)/\beta\), with bounded \(A_a,A_b\).
In the primary setting \(r\ge e^{-2B}\min r_*>0\).  The identities
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 x^\sharp=e^{a/2}\xi_*S^{-1},\qquad
 y^\sharp=e^{-b/2}Sy_*,\\
 X=x^\sharp+a_zu^*-u^*Z,\qquad Y=y^\sharp+Zv-b_zv,\\
 Z=S^{-1}f_zS^{-1},\qquad
 u=e^{a/2}S^{-1}\phi^*,\qquad v=e^{-b/2}S\psi.
 \end{gathered}
\]
then reconstruct both endpoint derivatives from the arrow kinetics and
\(DM\).  Here \(\xi_*,y_*\) remain the fixed reference derivatives,
whereas \(x^\sharp,y^\sharp\) depend on the current metric variables.
Set
\[
 A_x=\sup_X|\xi_*|^2/g,\qquad A_y=\sup_X|y_*|^2/g,
\]
the fixed intrinsic reference contractions.
For example
\(|\nabla a|^2\le12K_0/\alpha+6e^{2B}A_x/\alpha+3e^{4B}G_M\).
Writing \(r_{\min}=e^{-2B}\min r_*\), the same three-term square
inequality in \(b_zv=y^\sharp+Zv-Y\) gives explicitly
\[
 |\nabla b|^2\le12K_2/r_{\min}
                  +6e^{2B}A_y/r_{\min}+3e^{4B}G_M.
\]
The factors use \(\|Z\|\le e^{2B}\|M_z\|\),
\(p>\alpha\), and \(r\ge r_{\min}\).
Thus \(\Psi=\rho-a-b\) satisfies \(\Delta\Psi\ge aF-D\), where
\[
 F=|\nabla a|^2+G_M+|\nabla b|^2+U+W_1
      +1/q+K_0/q+1/\beta+K_2/\beta.
\]
Indeed subtracting the two endpoint rows gives
\(\Delta\Psi\ge a_MG_M+e^{-B}W_1+c_1e^{-B}U+c_0/q+K_0/q
 +A_0/\beta+K_2/\beta-D\).
Put \(C_g=1+6e^{4B}\), \(C_k=\max(12/\alpha,12/r_{\min})\),
and \(C_{\rm ref}=6e^{2B}(A_x/\alpha+A_y/r_{\min})\).
Since \(W_1\ge(K_0+K_2)/(c+d)\), the full Dirichlet density is at most
\(C_gG_M+C_k(c+d)W_1+C_{\rm ref}\).
The positive minimum of
\(a_M/C_g,e^{-B}/(C_k(c+d)+1),c_1e^{-B},c_0,A_0,1\)
therefore supplies \(a>0\), enlarging \(D\) by \(aC_{\rm ref}\).

In the boundary setting that bottom reconstruction is unavailable.
Instead use the genuine scalar potential \(\Psi_B=\rho-a+e^{-b}\).
Its exact bottom contribution is
\[
 \Delta e^{-b}=e^{-b}\left[-A_b+(C_2+K_2)/\beta+|b_z|^2/g\right].
\]
Consequently
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Delta\Psi_B\ge{}& a_MG_M+e^{-B}W_1+c_1e^{-B}U
 +(c_0+K_0)/q\\
 &{}+e^{-B}(A_0+K_2)/\beta
 +(e^{-B}/2)|\nabla b|^2-D,
 \quad c_0=55/63.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Only the top reconstruction is needed, and this again bounds the entire
\(F\) with a positive coefficient.  The oscillation of \(\Psi_B\) is
at most \(3(e^B-e^{-B})+2B\).  No lower norm is inserted.

Here and below the exact kernel device is
\begin{equation}\label{common-green-kernel}
 G_0(x,y)=\frac1{2\pi}\log
 \frac{|x_0y_1-x_1y_0|^2}{|x|^2|y|^2}\le0,
 \qquad \Delta_{{\rm FS},y}G_0\,\omega_{\rm FS}
 =\delta_x-\omega_{\rm FS}/(2\pi).
\end{equation}
Off the pole this follows by differentiation, and the logarithmic flux
gives its delta mass.  The smooth actual density converts the identity to
\(u(x)-\overline u_{\rm FS}=\int G_0(x,y)\Delta_Xu(y)\omega_X(y)\).
Also \(\int(-G_0)\omega_{\rm FS}=1\).
For the appropriate potential \(\Phi\),
\(m=\Delta\Phi+D\ge aF\ge0\) has
\(\int(-G_0)m=\bar\Phi_{\rm FS}-\Phi(x)+D\int(-G_0)\omega_X\).
The bounded oscillation (in the primary case at most
\(2(e^B-e^{-B})+4B\)) therefore gives,
uniformly for every center,
\begin{equation}\label{common-log-localization}
 \int(-G_0(x,y))F(y)\omega_X(y)\le H,
 \qquad \int_{B_s(x)}F\,\omega_X\le\frac{\pi H}{\log(1/s)}.
\end{equation}
The endpoints immediately give their two-sided component-source bounds.
For the matrix use the full ordered equation
\[
 \Delta f=g^{-1}f_{\bar z}f^{-1}f_z+df+tfM
                         -S\mathcal L_V^{-1}(C_1+K_1)S.
\]
Its first term has norm at most \(e^{3B}G_M/2\); the last term is
positive Hermitian before its minus sign and has norm at most
\(e^B(\|C_1\|_\infty U+W_1)\), by positivity and trace
self-adjointness.  Thus the full two-sided component-source bound is
\(|\Delta a|+|\Delta b|+\|\Delta f\|\le C(1+F)\).

Suppose the full gradient maxima \(G_n\) tend to infinity, attained at
\(z_n\).  A fixed chart and the scale \(y=G_n(z-z_n)\) give bounded
values and first derivatives on disks exhausting the plane.  By
\eqref{common-log-localization}, the Dirichlet energy on every such disk
tends to zero.  Every locally uniform value limit is therefore constant.
This is only a value assertion.  Derivative convergence below will always
come from a two-sided Poisson bound or a bounded \(\bar\partial\) source,
using Lemma~\ref{common-local-potentials}.

The same-point rank-one facts
\[
 V\ge(c-p)I=(2/3-q)I,\qquad\lambda_{\max}V\ge c
\]
give an exhaustive list: strict interior; strict \(V\) with one or both
scalar losses; matrix loss with strict \(\beta\); mixed matrix/bottom
loss.  A \(q\)-face cannot meet a matrix face.  At the boundary lower
zero, bounded values give \(P\to0\), hence \(\beta\to d\); that center
cannot be a bottom or mixed face.

\paragraph{Scalar faces with strict matrix symbol.}
Let \(T_R=\mathcal L_V^{-1}R,T_P=\mathcal L_V^{-1}P\).
The entire ordered scalar rows are
\begin{align}
 \Delta q={}&(2-p/q)K_0+\operatorname{tr}(T_RK_1)
 +\operatorname{tr}(T_RC_1)+t[pa-\operatorname{tr}(RM)]-pC_0/q,
 \label{common-q-row}\\
 \Delta\beta={}&-(2+r/\beta)K_2+\operatorname{tr}(T_PK_1)
 +\operatorname{tr}(T_PC_1)+t[rb-\operatorname{tr}(PM)]-rC_2/\beta.
 \label{common-beta-row}
\end{align}
The second row follows from
\(\Delta r=2K_2+rH_2-\operatorname{tr}(P\widehat H_1)\), with
trace self-adjointness, and has no \(q\) denominator.
Moreover \(q_z=Xu\) and \(\beta_z=-v^*Y\).
Strict \(V\) gives bounded two-sided first-scale sources for \(f\),
so its derivatives tend to zero.  Every strict endpoint does likewise.
One collapsing endpoint therefore retains a derivative witness:
\(q_z/G_n=pa_z/G_n+o(1)\), or
\(\beta_z/G_n=rb_z/G_n+o(1)\).
At a bottom face \(r\to d>0\); this local fact suffices even in the
boundary setting and at simultaneous scalar loss.

For \(q\le1/18\), \(V\ge11I/18\), \(p\le2/9\), and
\(0\le T_R\le p/(c-p)I\).  Decompose
\(K_0=|q_z|^2/(2gp)+K_{\perp}\).
For
\[
 F_q(q)=\int_0^q\frac{\sqrt s}{\alpha+s}\,ds,\qquad
 F_b(\beta)=\int_0^\beta\frac{\sqrt s}{d-s}\,ds,
\]
the logarithmic derivative ratios are
\(F_q''/F_q'=1/(2q)-1/p\) and
\(F_b''/F_b'=1/(2\beta)+1/r\).
Their chain terms cancel the singular parallel kinetics in the respective
rows.  In the top row the remaining upper perpendicular coefficient is
at most \(2-p/q+p/(c-p)\le-18/11\); in the bottom row the remaining
bottom perpendicular coefficient and bare bottom force are nonpositive.
The bounded other kinetic terms yield
\[
 \Delta F_q\le C\sqrt q(1+G_n^2),\qquad
 \Delta F_b\le C\sqrt\beta(1+G_n^2)
\]
in their respective neighborhoods.  If the selected scalar is \(s\),
put \(\epsilon_n=s(z_n)\) and scale by \(\epsilon_n/G_n\).
Then \(Q_n=s/\epsilon_n\) is positive, locally Lipschitz and centered
at one.  The divided transforms converge to positive multiples of
\(Q^{3/2}\); their upper sources tend to zero on every fixed disk,
including possible zero points.  The nonnegative entire superharmonic
limit is constant by Lemma~\ref{common-local-potentials}; hence \(Q=1\).
On the resulting disks \(Q_n\ge1/2\), the exact scalar row has bounded
two-sided normalized source.  The other scalar denominator is absent,
and \(V\) is buffered.  Poisson \(C^1\) compactness contradicts the
preserved derivative.  This excludes both single and simultaneous scalar
losses.  Strict interior is the direct componentwise Poisson case.

\paragraph{The full separated matrix row.}
Put \(\lambda=\lambda_{\min}V,\nu=\lambda_{\max}V\).
If \(\lambda<c/4\), then \(q\ge11/24,\nu\ge c\), and
\(\nu-\lambda\ge3c/4\).  In a separated eigenframe \(e,e'\), write
\[
 \rho_1=R_{ee},\quad\pi_1=P_{ee},\quad
 \zeta=R_{ee'}=P_{ee'},\quad s_1=\rho_1+\pi_1=c-\lambda+2\pi_1,
 \quad D=C_1+K_1.
\]
With \(X=(x_1,x_2),Y=(y_1,y_2)^T\), the eigenvalue concavity term is
\[
 C_{\rm eig}=
 \frac{|u_1x_2-y_1\bar v_2|^2+|u_2x_1-y_2\bar v_1|^2}
 {g(\nu-\lambda)}\ge0.
\]
Both squares are retained.  The ordered covariant row
\(\Delta_\nabla V=(YY^*-X^*X)/g+H_0R+H_2P-
\mathcal L_{R+P}\widehat H_1\) gives the all-point identity
\begin{align}
 \Delta\lambda={}&2(|y_1|^2-|x_1|^2)/(2g)
 +\rho_1(C_0+K_0)/q+\pi_1(C_2+K_2)/\beta-s_1D_{ee}/\lambda
 \notag\\[-2pt]
 &-4\operatorname{Re}(\zeta D_{e'e})/(\lambda+\nu)
 +t[\mathcal L_{R+P}M-aR-bP]_{ee}-C_{\rm eig},
 \qquad\lambda_z=-u_1x_1+y_1\bar v_1.
 \label{common-lambda-row}
\end{align}
It is not restricted to a minimum or to \(\lambda_z=0\).

For pure matrix loss, in the six real variables \(\mathbf w=(a,f,b)\)
the exact singular image is
\[
 \Delta\mathbf w=-mN_f+E,\qquad
 m=D_{ee}/\lambda,\quad N_f=(0,S\Pi_eS,0),\quad
 |E|\le C(1+G_n^2).
\]
Choose five smooth uniformly conditioned covectors annihilating \(N_f\)
at every current state and basepoint.  Their projected complex derivatives
have bounded \(\bar\partial\) source, as verified below for the
two-normal case.  Constant value limits imply weak limit zero; Cauchy
compactness then makes the projections uniformly zero in the limit.
Square-root transport gives \(d\lambda(N_f)=s_1\ge c-\lambda\).
Thus a nonzero full-gradient witness forces
\(|\lambda_z(z_n)|/G_n\ge k>0\).
The singular kinetic in \eqref{common-lambda-row} is
\(-s_1(|x_1|^2+|y_1|^2)/(2g\lambda)\), and
\(|\lambda_z|^2\le s_1(|x_1|^2+|y_1|^2)\).
All other coefficients are bounded, apart from nonpositive concavity.
Hence
\[
 \Delta\lambda\le-|\lambda_z|^2/(2g\lambda)+C(1+G_n^2).
\]
The transform \((2/3)\lambda^{3/2}\) cancels this derivative term.
The amplitude scale \(\lambda(z_n)/G_n\), entire superharmonic limit,
and exact two-sided row on \(Q_n\ge1/2\) contradict the witness exactly
as above.  Since \(s_1\ge c-\lambda\) even when \(P=0\), this includes
the boundary lower zero.

\paragraph{Moving projections at the mixed face.}
On \(\lambda<c/4,\beta<d/2\), the full equation is
\begin{equation}\label{common-mixed-image}
 \Delta\mathbf w=-mN_f-nN_b+E,
 \quad n=(C_2+K_2)/\beta,\quad N_b=(0,0,1),
 \quad |E|\le C(1+|D\mathbf w|^2).
\end{equation}
The whole kinetic singular image is included before projection.
Four smooth conditioned covectors \(\theta^j\) annihilating both normals
are obtained by applying
\(I-N(N^TN)^{-1}N^T\) to a constant four-frame with an invertible
limiting minor.  A smaller neighborhood bounds its Gram inverse and minor.
These forms need not be exact, and no common scalar first integrals are
asserted.  For \(W_n(y)=\mathbf w_n(z_n+y/G_n)\), put
\(j_n^j=\theta^j(W_n,z_n+y/G_n)\partial_yW_n\).
Direct differentiation, using \(\Delta=g^{-1}\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}\), gives
\begin{equation}\label{common-moving-annihilator}
 \partial_{\bar y}j_n^j
 =\theta^j g_nE_n/G_n^2
 +(D_w\theta^j)[\partial_{\bar y}W_n,\partial_yW_n]
 +(D_x\theta^j)[1/G_n,\partial_yW_n].
\end{equation}
The singular sources vanish exactly at moving states, not at a frozen
center.  The nonexact quadratic curl terms remain bounded.  Thus both real
divergence and curl are controlled through the complex source.  Cauchy
compactness and the distributionally zero derivatives of the constant
value limit make all four \(j_n^j\) locally uniformly tend to zero.
There is no error subsequently divided by \(\lambda\) or \(\beta\).

For completeness the differential conditioning retains transport.  If
\(\eta=S^{-1}\delta fS^{-1},T=\delta SS^{-1}\), and
\(\Omega=(T-T^*)/2\), then \(T+T^*=\eta\) and
\[
 \delta R=-\mathcal L_\eta R+[\Omega,R]+R\delta a,
 \qquad\delta P=\mathcal L_\eta P+[\Omega,P]-P\delta b.
\]
Pairing \(\delta V\) with \(\Pi_e\) kills only its commutator.
The normal derivative matrix is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{common-normal-conditioning}
 \begin{pmatrix}d\lambda(N_f)&d\lambda(N_b)\\
 d\beta(N_f)&d\beta(N_b)\end{pmatrix}
 =\begin{pmatrix}s_1&-\pi_1\\-\pi_1&r\end{pmatrix},
 \quad s_1r-\pi_1^2\ge(3c/4)(d/2)>0.
\end{equation}
Indeed the determinant is \((c-\lambda)r+2\pi_1r-\pi_1^2\).
The four annihilators together with \(d\lambda,d\beta\) form a bounded
invertible six-frame.  No integrability or bracket direction is lost.

\paragraph{Positive combined normals and all three ratios.}
For \(1<A<2\), set \(t_A=\lambda+A\beta\),
\(a_N=s_1-A\pi_1\), and \(b_N=Ar-\pi_1\).
Trace self-adjointness in \eqref{common-beta-row} gives the entire row
\begin{align}
 \Delta t_A={}&-a_N(C_1)_{ee}/\lambda-b_NC_2/\beta
 -a_N(K_1)_{ee}/\lambda-b_NK_2/\beta
 \notag\\
 &+2(|y_1|^2-|x_1|^2)/(2g)-2AK_2+\rho_1(C_0+K_0)/q
 +AP_{e'e'}D_{e'e'}/\nu
 \notag\\
 &+4(A-1)\operatorname{Re}(\zeta D_{e'e})/(\lambda+\nu)
 +t\{[\mathcal L_{R+P}M-aR-bP]_{ee}
       +A[rb-\operatorname{tr}(PM)]\}-C_{\rm eig}.
 \label{common-combined-row}
\end{align}
Here \(a_N\ge3c/4=5/8\) and \(b_N\ge(A-1)d/2\).
Both singular forces and kinetics are negative; the mixed entries are
bounded above, not assigned a false sign.  Since
\((t_A)_z=-u_1x_1+(1-A)\bar v_1y_1-A\bar v_2y_2\),
the three-term square inequality gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
 |(t_A)_z|^2\le K_At_A
 \left[a_N(|x_1|^2+|y_1|^2)/\lambda
       +b_N(|y_1|^2+|y_2|^2)/\beta\right],\\
 K_A=3\max\left(\frac{64}{15},\frac{(A-1)^2d}{5/8},
                              \frac{2A}{A-1}\right).
\end{gathered}
\]
Thus \(\Delta t_A\le-|(t_A)_z|^2/(2gK_At_A)+C(1+G_n^2)\).
For \(A_-=5/4,A_+=7/4\), a common \(K=30\) suffices.
The power \(F_A=t_A^{61/60}\) has logarithmic derivative ratio
\(1/(60t_A)\), and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{common-combined-power}
 \Delta F_A\le Ct_A^{1/60}(1+G_n^2).
\end{equation}

Let \(\delta_n=\lambda(z_n)+\beta(z_n)\) and use the shared scale
\(\ell_n=\delta_n/G_n\).  The functions
\(Q_\lambda=\lambda/\delta_n,Q_\beta=\beta/\delta_n\) are locally
uniformly Lipschitz.  Dividing \eqref{common-combined-power} by
\(\delta_n^{61/60}\) makes its upper rescaled source at most
\(C\delta_n(Q_\lambda+AQ_\beta)^{1/60}(1+G_n^{-2})\), which tends
to zero.  The two nonnegative entire transformed limits are constant.
The two distinct \(A\)'s force
\(Q_\lambda\to L,Q_\beta\to B_0\), with \(L,B_0\ge0,L+B_0=1\).
Also
\(\widetilde W_n=(\mathbf w_n(z_n+\ell_ny)-\mathbf w_n(z_n))/\delta_n\)
is Lipschitz and zero at the origin.  The four projected derivatives
vanish on these nested disks, and the two scalar gradients vanish
distributionally.  Coefficients freeze since state changes are
\(O(\delta_n)\).  The invertible frame
\eqref{common-normal-conditioning} forces every weak derivative of a
limit of \(\widetilde W_n\) to vanish; hence its value limit is zero.
Derivative preservation still requires the following three separate bridges.

If \(L,B_0>0\), both relative denominators are buffered.  The source
factor in the equations for \(\widetilde W_n\) is \(\delta_n/G_n^2\).
All six component Laplacians are bounded two-sided, so Poisson \(C^1\)
convergence contradicts the full-gradient witness at the origin.

If \(L=0,B_0=1\), choose five covectors annihilating only \(N_f\).
For \(J=\vartheta(\mathbf w,x)\mathbf w_z/G_n\) on the shared scale,
\[
 \partial_{\bar y}J=(\delta_n/G_n^2)\vartheta g_n\Delta\mathbf w
       +\delta_n O(1)+\ell_nO(1).
\]
The whole middle singular image cancels exactly, while the bottom source
is bounded because \(\delta_n/\beta\le2\) on fixed disks.
The weak zero limit supplied by \(\widetilde W_n\to0\), followed by
Cauchy compactness, gives \(J\to0\) uniformly.  The witness is therefore
in \(N_f\), and \(|\lambda_z(z_n)|/G_n\ge k>0\).
Now use the smaller scale \(\epsilon_n/G_n\),
\(\epsilon_n=\lambda(z_n)\).  The bottom symbol remains comparable
to \(\delta_n\), because its variation is \(O(\epsilon_n)\) and
\(\epsilon_n/\delta_n\to0\).  The exact matrix row yields
\[
 \Delta\lambda\le-|\lambda_z|^2/(2g\lambda)
          +C(1+G_n^2)(1+1/\beta).
\]
The transformed amplitude source is
\(C\epsilon_n\sqrt Q(1+G_n^{-2})(1+1/\beta)\to0\).
Entire Liouville gives \(Q=1\).  On \(Q_n\ge1/2\), the exact row has
bounded two-sided source; its bottom terms carry
\(\epsilon_n/\beta\to0\).  Poisson compactness contradicts the witness.
No unspecified \(o(1)/\lambda\) error is used.

If \(B_0=0,L=1\), the five components \((a,f)\) have bounded
two-sided shared-scale sources: they contain no bottom singularity and
\(\lambda/\delta_n\ge1/2\).  Their derivative limits are zero.
The witness is in \(b\), and
\(\beta_z=rb_z-v^*Zv-v^*y^\sharp\), with \(r\to d\), preserves a nonzero
\(\beta_z/G_n\).  On the smaller scale
\(\epsilon_n/G_n,\epsilon_n=\beta(z_n)\), the matrix symbol remains
comparable to \(\delta_n\).  The exact bottom transform gives
\(\Delta F_b\le C\sqrt\beta(1+G_n^2)(1+1/\lambda)\).
Its amplitude source tends to zero through
\(\epsilon_n/\lambda\to0\); Liouville gives \(Q=1\), and the exact
two-sided bottom row on \(Q_n\ge1/2\) contradicts the witness.
These three ratios exhaust the mixed face.  At a boundary mixed center
\(r\ge d/2\) locally, so the lower zero is already excluded without a
global lower norm.  The gradient bound is proved in both settings.

\paragraph{Separate actual minima.}
All kinetics are now bounded.  At an actual small global \(q\)-minimum,
the same-point \(V\) buffer and \eqref{common-q-row} give
\(0\le\Delta q\le C-\alpha c_0/q\), proving the top gap.
First minimize \(\lambda+(3/2)\beta\).  A minimum tending to zero lies
in a separated mixed chart.  The exact combined row gives there
\[
 0\le\Delta(\lambda+(3/2)\beta)
 \le-(5/8)c_1/\lambda-(d/4)A_0/\beta+C,
\]
a contradiction.  Hence this total normal is at least \(\delta_t>0\).
At an actual \(\lambda\)-minimum
\(\epsilon<\min(c/4,\delta_t/2)\), its same-point bottom symbol is
at least \(\delta_t/3\).  The full matrix row gives
\(0\le\Delta\lambda\le-s_1c_1/\epsilon+C\), so \(V\) has a gap.
At an actual \(\beta\)-minimum below
\(\min(d/2,\delta_t/3)\), its same-point matrix symbol is at least
\(\delta_t/2\); the ordered probe is bounded and
\(0\le\Delta\beta\le-(d/2)A_0/\beta+C\).  This gives the bottom gap.
The minimizing points were never synchronized.  Repeated eigenvalues
cause no differentiability issue because every small matrix-normal minimum
has \(\nu-\lambda\ge3c/4\).  At a lower zero \(\beta=d\).
head: environment

label: common-anchor
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{common-anchor}
For each of the two fixed settings, there is one finite mass \(\mu_s\),
chosen independently of every later lower cutoff \(\tau_-\), with a smooth
\(C^{2,\gamma}\)-valued auxiliary solution curve on \([\tau_b,1]\),
through \((1,0)\).  At \(\tau_b>0\) its solution is unique among all
positive-symbol solutions and has an invertible unrestricted derivative.
Its normalized derivative is also an isomorphism.
head: environment
name: Signed upper branch and all-solution anchor

title: Proof
body_md:
There are two tasks at the anchor parameter: construct a nearby
solution with invertible derivative, and show that no other
positive-symbol solution occurs there. The latter is needed to identify
the degree of the whole bounded solution domain with the nonzero local
index. Neither task asserts uniqueness below the anchor.

Let \(L=\|F_{*1}\|_{\infty,\mathrm{op}}\), let
\(T_+=1\) if \(L=0\) and
\(T_+=\min(1,A_0/(2L))\) otherwise, and set \(\tau_b=T_+/2\).
Then \(C_1^\tau\ge A_0I/2\) on \([0,T_+]\); no such sign is needed
on the whole upper interval.  Write the entire remainder as
\[
 \mathcal R_t(w)=\widehat F(w)-F_*-J_*w+t(B(w)-A_*)w.
\]
The equation is
\(L_tw=-(1-\tau)F_*-\mathcal R_t(w)\).
On a fixed small value neighborhood all finite coefficient derivatives
of the exponential, inverse, square root, arrows, and transported curvature
are bounded.  The remainder consists of: coefficient variation times
\(D^2w\); quadratic first derivatives; variations multiplying a single
first derivative; the zeroth Taylor remainder; and mass variation.
Hölder multiplication on a weighted radius \(R\), with \(R/t\le r_0\),
gives term by term
\[
 \|\mathcal R_t(w)\|_\gamma\le C_NR^2/t,
 \qquad
 \|\mathcal R_t(w)-\mathcal R_t(z)\|_\gamma
 \le C_NR/t\,\|w-z\|_{t,\gamma}.
\]
For instance the first product is
\(O(\|w\|_\gamma\|D^2w\|_\gamma)\), the second
\(O(\|Dw\|_\gamma^2)\), and the mass product
\(O(t\|w\|_\gamma^2)\); each is \(O(R^2/t)\).
Difference products give the second inequality in the same weighted norm.
This does not require small unweighted second derivatives.

Take \(C_I\ge1\),
\[
 R=2C_I(\|F_*\|_\gamma+1),\qquad
 t_{\rm req}=\max(t_0,1,R/r_0,4C_IC_NR).
\]
For \(t\ge t_{\rm req}\),
\(-L_t^{-1}[(1-\tau)F_*+\mathcal R_t(w)]\) maps the complete
radius-\(R\) ball to itself and contracts by at most \(1/4\).
Geometric iteration constructs its unique fixed point.  At \(\tau=1\)
that point is zero.  Value closeness gives
\(q\ge5/21,\beta\ge23/30,V\ge2I/21\) after enlarging the threshold.
For a fixed finite mass the weighted norms are uniformly equivalent on
\([\tau_b,1]\).  The resolvent identity and uniform contraction give
continuity, and the factorization
\[
 D_w\mathcal E=L_t[I+L_t^{-1}D\mathcal R_t(w_\tau)]
\]
has a norm-convergent inverse.  Difference quotients and repeated
differentiation give the smooth curve, with one-sided endpoint derivatives.
Exact total integration gives \(tN(w)=0\) after construction.

It remains to place every solution at the anchor in that ball.
On the positive-force slab Lemma~\ref{common-positive-size} gives
\(\|w\|_\infty\le C_W/t\), independently of any solution selection.
For large \(t\) this buffers all symbols near the reference.
In a chart set \(y=\sqrt t(x-x_0),W=tw\).  The complete normalized
equation \eqref{common-scalar-principal} is
\[
 \Delta_yW=4g(x)\{W-H(x,W/t,\tau)
       -t^{-1/2}B_1(x,W/t)[D_yW]
       -t^{-1}Q_1(x,W/t)[D_yW,D_yW]\}.
\]
If \(G_n=\sqrt{t_n}\|Dw_n\|_\infty\to\infty\), rescale again
by \(\sqrt{t_n}G_n\) at an attaining point.  The rescaled values are
bounded, all gradients are bounded with a nonzero central witness, and
the full Laplacian is
\[
 4g_n\{(\widetilde W_n-H_n)/G_n^2
       -B_{1,n}[D\widetilde W_n]/(\sqrt{t_n}G_n)
       -Q_{1,n}[D\widetilde W_n,D\widetilde W_n]/t_n\}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The domains exhaust the plane.  Local Poisson compactness preserves the
gradient witness in \(C^1\), whereas the bounded harmonic six-vector
limit is constant: its derivative is at most \(C\|W\|_\infty/R\)
on arbitrary disks.  This is a contradiction.  A finite threshold follows
also directly from
\(|DU(0)|\le C_P(\|U\|_\infty/R+R\|\Delta U\|_\infty)\):
first choose a fixed \(R\) to make the value term less than one quarter
of the witness, then large \(G,t\) to make each of the three source terms
less than one quarter.  Thus \(\|Dw\|_\infty\le C_G/\sqrt t\).

On first-scale disks bounded values, gradients and Laplacians give
\(C^{1,\nu}\) bounds for any \(\gamma<\nu<1\), and then
\(C^{2,\gamma}\) bounds by the Hessian cancellation estimate.
Rescaling and the finite atlas give
\[
 \|w\|_\gamma\le C_St^{-1+\gamma/2},\quad
 \|Dw\|_\gamma\le C_St^{-1/2+\gamma/2},\quad
 \|D^2w\|_\gamma\le C_St^{\gamma/2}.
\]
Farther point pairs are controlled by the corresponding supremum divided
by the first-scale radius to power \(\gamma\).  The complete original
remainder consequently satisfies
\(\|\mathcal R_t(w)\|_\gamma\le C_Rt^{-(1-\gamma)}\):
the coefficient--Hessian, gradient-square and mass terms have precisely
this order, and linear-gradient and zeroth remainders decay faster.
The mass-uniform inverse then puts every solution in the same contraction
ball for a finite \(T_{\rm all}\).  Choose once
\[
 \mu_s\ge\max(t_{\rm req},T_{\rm all})/\tau_b.
\]
At the anchor all positive-symbol solutions therefore coincide with the
constructed one.  Differentiating the exact total identity there gives
\(\int\operatorname{tr}_{\rm tot}(D_w\mathcal E\,U)=tDN(w)U\).
The unrestricted inverse restricts to an isomorphism
\(\ker DN(w)\to Y\).  No simplicity premise or kernel classification
has been used.  For the boundary setting all constants are recomputed
from its smooth zero-safe coefficients; no primary uniformity across
rank loss is asserted.

label: common-positive-continuation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{common-positive-continuation}
For each fixed primary setting, and separately for each fixed
lower-boundary setting, the mass chosen in Lemma~\ref{common-anchor}
has a connected subset of smooth normalized positive-symbol auxiliary
solutions containing \((1,0)\) and projecting onto all \((0,1]\).
There is no assertion of a single-valued curve below the anchor,
uniqueness there, a nested choice of components, or compactness at zero.
head: environment
name: Positive-parameter continuation at one fixed mass

title: Proof
body_md:
First fix a positive lower cutoff and use degree invariance to obtain a
solution on every parameter slice. Slice-wise existence alone does not
give the connected set in the statement. A compact zero-set argument
then shows that the component through the anchor reaches the lower
cutoff. Finally, the components for different cutoffs can be joined
through that same anchor, without requiring them to be nested or
single-valued.

Fix \(0<\tau_-<\tau_b\), without changing \(\mu_s\).
The independent estimate \(B_{\tau_-}=C_{\rm size}/(\tau_-\mu_s)\) applies
to every solution on this interval, even before existence is known.
Theorem~\ref{common-gradient-gaps} with \(c_1=A_0/2\) gives all
stage gradients and gaps.  The zero-safe boundary localization, rather
than the primary positive-lower-norm step, supplies this inference in
the boundary setting.

Let \(E=C^{1,\gamma}(X;\mathbb R\oplus\operatorname{Herm}(2)
\oplus\mathbb R)\), and choose one fixed finite \(\kappa\ge1\)
large enough for the scalar Gaussian/localization construction above.
Applied componentwise, that construction gives the bounded scalar inverse
\(S_\kappa=(-\Delta+\kappa)^{-1}\) on all six fields.  Define
\[
 K_\tau(w)=S_\kappa[(\kappa-\tau\mu_s)w+G(x,w,Dw,\tau)].
\]
Its fixed points are exactly the full equations
\eqref{common-scalar-principal}; a \(C^{1,\gamma}\) fixed point gains
\(C^{2,\gamma}\), and normalization follows afterwards.  Stage values,
gradients and gaps give uniform \(C^{2,\nu}\) zero-set bounds for every
fixed \(\gamma<\nu<1\): the bounded component source first gives
\(C^{1,\sigma}\), \(\nu<\sigma<1\), then the complete smooth source
is \(C^{0,\nu}\), and the local Hessian estimate gives \(C^{2,\nu}\).
Choose \(R_{\tau_-}\) strictly above the zero-set \(C^{1,\gamma}\) bound and
\(0<\epsilon_{\tau_-}<\frac12\min(\delta_{q,\tau_-},
\delta_{\beta,\tau_-},\delta_{V,\tau_-})\).  The bounded open set
\[
 \Omega_{\tau_-}=\{\|w\|_{C^{1,\gamma}}<R_{\tau_-},
                q>\epsilon_{\tau_-},\ \beta>\epsilon_{\tau_-},
                V>\epsilon_{\tau_-} I\}
\]
has legal closure and no fixed point on its boundary.
On this bounded buffered domain the images of \(K_\tau\) have a uniform
\(C^{2,\gamma}\) bound, hence are jointly precompact in \(E\) by
Ascoli and lower-exponent interpolation.  The forcing is affine in
\(\tau\), so parameter dependence is uniformly Lipschitz there.
The exact zero set is compact even in
\([\tau_-,\tau_b]\times C^{2,\gamma}\).  Convexity and an invariant-domain
property are unnecessary.

We use the compact-map degree and local index of Leray and
Schauder~\cite{LS1934}, in their cited 1934 journal edition.
Sections 4--8, 10--11, and 12--16 supply the degree for
\(I-K\) on bounded open real Banach domains with compact maps and no
boundary zeros, its existence, excision, additivity and compact-homotopy
invariance, and the nondegenerate local index \(\pm1\).
The application here is to the bounded legal domains just checked, not
to a global map on the whole Banach space; neither the weak-compactness
discussion in section 9 nor the global-map discussion in section 17 is
an additional premise.  These source degree/index properties, including
their finite-dimensional degree background, are the external input;
all analytic hypotheses and the component application are proved here.

At the unique anchor, \(DK\) is compact.  A kernel element of
\(I-DK\) gains \(C^{2,\gamma}\) and solves the actual full linearization,
so Lemma~\ref{common-anchor} makes it zero.  The compact Fredholm
alternative required here has a direct proof.  If \(A=I-C\), with
\(C\) compact, is injective but not bounded below, a unit sequence with
\(Ax_n\to0\) has a convergent subsequence through \(Cx_n\), contradicting
injectivity.  Thus its range and all \(R_n=A^nE\) are closed.  If it is
not onto, every inclusion \(R_{n+1}\subset R_n\) is strict: equality
at one stage, canceled using injectivity of \(A^n\), would give \(AE=E\).
Choose unit \(x_n\in R_n\) at distance greater than \(1/2\) from
\(R_{n+1}\): for \(y\) outside that proper closed subspace, put
\(d_0=\operatorname{dist}(y,R_{n+1})>0\), take
\(z\in R_{n+1}\) with \(\|y-z\|<2d_0\), and normalize \(y-z\).
For \(n>m\), both \(Cx_n\) and \(Ax_m\) belong to \(R_{m+1}\), so
\(\|Cx_m-Cx_n\|>1/2\), contradicting compactness.  Hence \(A\) is
onto with bounded inverse, without an approximation-property premise.
The local linear homotopy is zero-free on a sufficiently small sphere:
if the nonlinear error is at most
\(\|h\|/(2\|A^{-1}\|)\), it cannot cancel \(Ah\).
Thus the external local index result gives \(\pm1\).
Anchor uniqueness and excision make the degree on \(\Omega_{\tau_-}\)
nonzero.  The checked compact zero-free homotopy preserves it, yielding
solutions on every stage slice.

For the stronger component conclusion, let \(\mathcal S\) be this compact
zero set and \(p=(\tau_b,w_b)\).  The equivalence class \(P_n\) of
\(p\) under finite chains of steps less than \(1/n\) is clopen in
\(\mathcal S\), compact, and nested.  Their intersection is the component
of \(p\): it is connected, since a separation of the compact intersection
into two disjoint compact neighborhoods with positive distance would,
by nested compactness, eventually contain \(P_n\) in their union, whereas
a sufficiently small-step chain cannot cross that distance.  Conversely
every connected set through \(p\) lies in every clopen \(P_n\).
If this component misses the \(\tau_-\)-slice, nested compactness gives
some \(P_n\) missing that slice.  A small relative product neighborhood
\(\mathcal O\) isolates exactly this selected compact clopen zero set,
with no zero on its relative boundary.

The degree of the moving slice \(\mathcal O_\tau\) is locally constant.
Indeed at any nonempty selected slice choose a bounded open \(U\) whose
closure lies in \(\mathcal O_{\tau_0}\) and contains precisely its compact
selected zeros.  For nearby parameters its closure remains in
\(\mathcal O_\tau\), all selected zeros remain in \(U\), and there are no
boundary zeros; otherwise compactness produces a contradicting limiting
zero.  Excision reduces the moving-slice degree to that on \(U\), and
fixed-domain homotopy invariance proves constancy.  Empty selected slices
stay empty nearby by the same compactness argument.  This degree would
be zero at \(\tau_-\) but \(\pm1\) at \(\tau_b\), a contradiction.
Thus the anchor component \(C_{\tau_-}\) meets \(\tau_-\), and its connected
projection contains \([\tau_-,\tau_b]\).
On the compact zero set the identity between the \(C^{2,\gamma}\) and
\(C^{1,\gamma}\) topologies is a compact-to-Hausdorff homeomorphism,
so this is also a \(C^{2,\gamma}\) component.

Join every \(C_{\tau_-}\) to the already constructed upper curve.  All share
the same anchor at the same mass.  A union of connected sets sharing one
point is connected, and its projection is \((0,1]\).  No nesting,
coherent graph, limit exchange, or compact global union is used.
The smooth scalar-principal bootstrap makes every fixed point smooth.

label: common-trace-bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{common-trace-bound}
Every positive-parameter auxiliary solution in either fixed setting has
\(T\le C_T\), independently of mass, parameter, force sign, values,
derivatives and symbol minima.  The same bound holds for an actual
normalized zero-parameter solution, if one exists.
head: environment
name: Uniform upper radial trace

title: Proof
body_md:
The total source mean is zero.  Define
\(z_{\rm raw}(x)=\int G_0(x,y)f_*(y)\omega_X(y)\) and subtract its
actual mean to obtain \(z\).  The constant term in the kernel identity
vanishes against the total source mean, so \(\Delta_Xz=f_*\).
Local logarithmic potentials for its smooth source, and their harmonic
remainders, show successively that \(z\) is smooth.
With \(n_\omega=\sup\omega_X/\omega_{\rm FS}\), kernel integrability
gives \(\|z\|_\infty\le2n_\omega\|f_*\|_\infty\).
Set \(Z=(1-\tau)z,D=T-Z\).  The exact trace equation gives
\(\Delta D=tv\ge tT=t(D+Z)\).  At a global maximum of \(D\),
\(D\le\|Z\|_\infty\); hence \(T\le2\|z\|_\infty=:C_T\).
The resulting bound contains no factor \(1/t\).  At zero, if an actual normalized solution
exists, \(T-z\) is a constant \(C\); since
\(\int v=0\), \(v\ge T\), and \(\int z=0\), one has \(C\le0\).
This proves only the stated trace interface, not a full value bound.
